# Part I: Find the Data

## Story Pitch

A basketball player playing in a professional basketball league overseas
is frustrated with his current role on the team. Playing time for him is
scarce, and is only entered into the game for certain situations rather
than consistently. He’s wondering when he will get an opportunity to
show off his talent more. After another frustrating outing, the player
goes home and looks up data on unexpected NBA performances from players
who took on a similar role to his. The dataset contains the name of the
player, statistics including but not limited to points, assists,
rebounds, and steals, the date of the performance, the team the player
played against, and which career game it was for them. The main data
points will be the number of points scored and how late into the
player's career it was.

Through the use of this data, a correlation can be made between the
player’s experience with playing and a breakout performance, and a
prediction can be made of when a breakout performance will happen.
Additionally, with the data, the impact of the performance in connection
to future factors like pay raises, improvements in life, and trades to
nicer places can be analyzed. This data is significant because in most
professional leagues, there is a significant gap in success between
players who play a certain role on a team, versus a superstar, and a
person who’s just on the team. Role players still have an impact on the
team and are important. However, they are still some of the more
overlooked individuals on a team. For our investigation, we’re choosing
to take on the perspective of someone in the middle, which is a role
player, and see if we can make any connections and predictions of said
player’s career and quality of life afterward.

Most basketball players—regardless of level—at some point in their
career struggle. Everyone starts at the bottom, and some don’t even make
it to the top. However, more data analysis of players who have been in
similar situations can serve as motivation for others experiencing
hardship and can also be used to make predictions about the
possibilities of career turnaround, significant changes, and when a
breakout game will happen. An ‘unexpected performance’ in this case is
the event of a player scoring a high number of points, atypical to their
usual performance. In the dataset, every single player is a role player
or a niche player who did not have much of a spotlight shone on them,
yet scored a high number of points in contrast to their typical
performance. For these types of players, and to a normie basketball fan,
it is often assumed that they will never become a big player or have a
significant career worth remembering. Despite this, regardless of how
popular the player is, an ‘unexpected’ scoring game can be life-changing
for a player, leading to significant career changes such as paycheck
raises and an increased role on the team. However, this isn’t always the
case. Through the story of our basketball player, the information taken
from the dataset will be used to predict a breakout game and whether or
not the performance likely results in significant changes in the
player’s career.

### "Why the Data"

The target audience for our data analysis would most likely be
basketball fans with an interest in statistics and numbers or people
with a background or interest in data science, statistics, or any sort
of data analysis. There is also a small group of people who are both
basketball fans and statistics fans. Usually, these people do sports
analytics for either sports betting or for live data during
intermissions. Standard basketball fans most likely would not be
interested; they would be more interested in the game itself. Anyone
who’s interested in statistics, data science, and data analysis would
most likely be engaged. For this project, we will focus on the small
group that is sports analytics.

The unexpected is a big interest for statistics in general. True
“randomness” is incredibly complicated and requires highly intricate
algorithms just to return a pseudo-random integer. This is what
separates humans from computers: the ability to raise the unexpected.
Most basketball players, after playing enough games, have a general
expected skill. But the interesting stuff, as the video showcases, are
the players who suddenly have an unexpectedly high output for a game.
Could there be a pattern in the data?

### "About the Data"

We downloaded our dataset from The Pudding’s GitHub repository. This
dataset contains 1,703 observations (rows), and each row represents one
NBA player and their most unexpected game performance. The dataset
contains 19 features (columns). Some features we could find in another
dataset include player ID, season, and year. We could use these features
to connect our dataset with NBA player salary data. Through this, we can
explore whether players received salary increases after their unexpected
performances.

# Part II: Data Join

## Importing libraries/packages

```{r}
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
```

## Loading dataframes

```{r}
the_pudding_df <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/the-pudding/data/master/nba-unexpected/nba.csv", sep = ",")
bbrID_to_playerID <- read.csv("id-crosswalk.csv")
kaggle_player_stats_df <- read.csv("PlayerStatistics.csv")
```

## Joining Data

```{r}
kaggle_with_bbrID_df <- inner_join(kaggle_player_stats_df, bbrID_to_playerID, join_by(personId == nbaID), relationship = "many-to-many")

kaggle_with_bbrID_df <-
  kaggle_with_bbrID_df |>
  mutate(cleanedDates = substr(gameDateTimeEst, 1, 10))

unexpected_players_df <- inner_join(
  the_pudding_df, kaggle_with_bbrID_df, 
  join_by(
    bbrID, 
    Date == cleanedDates))

total_num_rows <- nrow(unexpected_players_df)

dataframe <- left_join(the_pudding_df, kaggle_with_bbrID_df, join_by(bbrID))
missing_data_df <-
  dataframe |>
  filter(is.na(personId))

estimated_margin_of_error <- 
  round(nrow(missing_data_df) / nrow(the_pudding_df) * 100, 2)
paste("Estimated margin of error: ", estimated_margin_of_error, "%")
```

Columns:

- bbrID, Date, Tm, Opp, TRB, AST, STL, BLK, PTS, GmSc, Season, Playoffs,
  Year, GameIndex, GmScMovingZ, GmScMovingZTop2Delta, Date2, GmSc2,
  GmScMovingZ2, firstName, lastName, personId, gameId, gameDateTimeEst,
  playerteamCity, playerteamName, opponentteamCity, opponentteamName,
  gameType, gameLabel, gameSubLabel, seriesGameNumber, win, home,
  numMinutes, points, assists, blocks, steals, fieldGoalsAttempted,
  fieldGoalsPercentage, threePointersAttempted, threePointersMade,
  threePointersPercentage, freeThrowsAttempted, freeThrowsMade,
  freeThrowsPercentage, reboundsDefensive, reboundsOffensive,
  reboundsTotal, foulsPersonal, turnovers, plusMinusPoints,
  playerteamId, opponentteamId, comment, startingPosition, gameDate

Total number of rows: `r total_num_rows`

# Part 3: Data Documentation

The first dataset records the players’ data from that unexpected NBA
game. To get a detailed understanding of the data structure, let’s take
a look at the README file of the first dataset on GitHub to understand
what its columns mean.

GitHub url:
https://github.com/the-pudding/data/blob/master/nba-unexpected/README.md

The readme file of this dataset not only shows the column names and
their meanings in detail, but also shows the source of the dataset, how
it was collected, and the author’s contact information.

The second dataset shows all the games played by every NBA player, and
the data is more detailed and larger in size. Unfortunately, this
dataset doesn’t come with a readme file, but as a substitute, you can
view the dataset online by selecting files in the webpage display
section, and each column has detailed notes (not the abbreviations in
the downloadable version). So, using this method, we can understand the
data in each specific column.

Kaggle url:
https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/eoinamoore/historical-nba-data-and-player-box-scores?resource=download&select=PlayerStatistics.csv

After merging the two data sets, we decided to pick out some important
variables as preliminary analysis information. We think
bbrID(basketball-reference player id), personId(person id), gameId(game
id), gameDateTimeEst(game date time EST), GmScMovingZ(z-score of game
from moving average), points(points), opponentteamName(opponent team
name), playerteamName(player team name), gameType(game type), home(home
game), numMinutes(minutes played), startingPosition(starting position),
GameIndex(game number in career), Season(season). The most meaningful
ones are GmScMovingZ and points, because these two variables directly
define the ‘unexpected outbreak relative to the usual level’ and are the
core of the project data. Next are numMinutes, startingPosition, home,
gameType, opponentteamName, playerteamName, GameIndex, and Season,
because they are the most useful explanatory variables for analyzing the
reasons behind unexpected scores.

These columns cover the identifiers needed for merging data, the core
metrics that define ‘unexpected,’ as well as potential factors like
playing time, role, home or away games, match types, opponent teams, and
career stage, which are enough to support analyzing the causes of role
players’ breakthroughs. We’ll use this data for further analysis (and
will also appropriately use other columns to help verify or add
factors).

Limitations and bias: This dataset lacks information on teammates’
status, coaching decisions and tactical role changes, opponents’
tactical setups, and environmental factors at the game. It also doesn’t
include descriptions of players’ condition or events on the day of the
match. This database is public and highly anonymized, supporting
privacy, transparency, and explainability. However, it lacks clear
accountability mechanisms and standards for safe use, and fairness and
non-discrimination tests are also insufficient (possibly because the
collected information is biased towards certain
teams/players/ethnicities, based on personal preferences). Human
oversight of the technology, professional responsibility, and safeguards
for promoting human values are also unclear.

In summary, the data does a great job in making information transparent
and clarifying the meaning of the data, but it lacks an explanation of
where the data comes from and the criteria for collecting the
information (for example, what standard counts as an unexpected score
and can be included in the information).
